Which big GPU cloud is cheapest for H100 and B200? On each provider's own pricing page on November 3, 2026: for the H100, Crusoe at $3.90 per GPU-hour on demand, with Lambda a cent behind at $3.99 on an 8-GPU instance. For the B200, Lambda at $6.69 per GPU-hour (8x), well under Nebius ($8.50) and CoreWeave ($8.60). CoreWeave is the most expensive on demand, but if your job can be interrupted its published spot prices ($2.46 an H100, $4.26 a B200, per GPU) undercut everyone's on-demand rate. Two dates to know: Crusoe's own page says its H100 goes to $4.50 on December 1, 2026, which hands the cheapest on-demand H100 to Lambda.

## The short answer (read Nov 3, 2026)

Among CoreWeave, Nebius, Lambda and Crusoe, the cheapest on-demand H100 on November 3, 2026 was Crusoe at $3.90 per GPU-hour, then Lambda at $3.99 (8x instance), Nebius at $4.50 and CoreWeave at $6.16 (an 8-GPU node at $49.24 an hour). Crusoe's page says its H100 rises to $4.50 on December 1, 2026. The cheapest on-demand B200 was Lambda at $6.69 per GPU-hour (8x; $6.99 on one GPU), then Nebius at $8.50 and CoreWeave at $8.60; Crusoe's B200 is contact-sales. For interruptible work, CoreWeave's spot nodes work out to $2.46 per H100 and $4.26 per B200, and Nebius preemptible starts from $0.79 (H100) and $0.99 (B200) at a dynamic rate. Smaller clouds go lower still: Hyperstack listed a B200 at $6.00 and an H100 at $2.50.

results.title: ISSUE #7: The B300 Trickle
results.author: Bobby Clay
highlights:
Published August 25, 2026 · Pricing evidence through August 24, 2026 · Ornn Compute Price Index (OCPI) through August 23, 2026, 20:00 UTC.

...

The one-line read. The four public floors did not move this week: H100 SXM $3.85, H200 $4.29, B200 $6.69, A100 SXM4 $2.30, the same levels we have shown since mid-July. Two things moved around them. The OCPI transaction index rose under three of the four floors, narrowing every gap on the board. And the B300, a chip that has been shipping since last year, is still finding a public price: only a few clouds list it on-demand, intermittently, and where they do the numbers range from about $7.85 to about $26.15 per GPU-hour. A settled floor, a firming index underneath it, and an established Blackwell GPU whose public price is still a trickle. 

## This week 

- Floors held. All four board floors are unchanged: H100 SXM $3.85 (Nebius), H200 $4.29 (Crusoe), B200 $6.69 (Lambda), A100 SXM4 $2.30 (Crusoe), the same levels we have published since mid-July. Across all nine indexed providers, no comparable public on-demand rate moved more than 1% week over week.
- The index moved under them. The floors held, but the OCPI transaction index did not. Week over week it rose for H100 ($2.64 to $2.87), B200 ($5.93 to $6.64), and A100 SXM4 ($1.02 to $1.07), and fell for H200 ($4.75 to $4.42). With the floors flat, every gap on the board narrowed. B200’s floor is now just $0.05 above the index, the tightest spread on the board.
- The B300 trickle. The B300 is an established Blackwell-generation GPU, in market since last year, with prior history in the AIForge Works catalog. What is still catching up is its public price. Only a handful of clouds list it on-demand, and they do so intermittently: AWS’s eight-GPU p6-b300.48xlarge appeared in Seoul for the first time in our reviewed history this week (Linux and four licensed operating-system variants), while Nebius listings dropped and then returned. We now see publicly listed on-demand B300 rates from three providers, AWS, OCI, and Nebius; CoreWeave shows the SKU but its rate is still contact-sales. The listed rates disagree sharply, from about $7.85 per GPU-hour (Nebius, three regions) to about $26.15 (AWS, Seoul). That is catalog visibility, not orderable capacity, and it is what a chip still finding its public price looks like.

...

A flat floor can look like a market asleep. This week it was the opposite. The four numbers you would take into a renewal did not move, H100 $3.85, H200 $4.29, B200 $6.69, A100 SXM4 $2.30. But the OCPI transaction index rose under three of them, and B200’s floor went from $0.76 above the index a week ago to $0.05 above it now. The catalog floor held; the transactional market moved up to meet it. That is a firming market, not a soft one, and it is the kind of thing a single weekly number would miss if it only reported the floor.

results.title: Crusoe Alternative (2026): GPU Prices vs PowerGPU
highlights:
Crusoe (founded 2018 by Chase Lochmiller and Cully Cavness) began as a Digital Flare Mitigation business, converting natural gas that oil wells would otherwise burn off into on-site power for mobile data centers, and used that power first to mine bitcoin before selling the mining/DFM unit to NYDIG in late 2024 to focus entirely on AI cloud. Crusoe Cloud now sells on-demand GPU instances — H100, H200, A100 and L40S on a published rate card, plus AMD MI300X — while Blackwell-class B200, GB200 NVL72 and AMD's MI355X are contact-sales only, alongside Managed Kubernetes, Managed Slurm and S3-compatible storage. The company is also building gigawatt-scale "AI Factory" campuses, including a large site in Abilene, Texas, sold separately as dedicated capacity.

results.title: GPU Rental Prices Are Rising Again: What the October 2026 Nebius and AWS Changes Mean for Inference Cost
highlights:
After falling in 2025, H100 rental prices rose in 2026. Nebius raised list prices on 1 October and AWS raised Capacity Blocks on 7 October. Here is what the numbers show and how to plan for them.

...

Published Sep 15, 2026 · Updated Oct 21, 2026

In short

- GPU rental prices fell in 2025 and are rising in 2026. Nebius raised its H100 on-demand price from $3.85 to $4.50 per GPU-hour on 1 October 2026.
- AWS raised EC2 Capacity Blocks prices by about 15% in October. AWS on-demand prices did not change.
- One price index put the median on-demand H100 SXM at $4.20 per GPU-hour on 7 October 2026. Hyperscalers charged a median of $10.53 for the same GPU.
- The "price per GPU-hour" you see is a list price. Your real cost per token depends on utilization, and a half-idle GPU costs twice as much per token.
- Plan for price drift: use commitments for steady load, keep workloads portable, and track cost per token, not cost per hour.

For most of 2025 the story was falling GPU prices. In October 2026 the direction has changed. This article looks at what was published in the first three weeks of the month, what the sources say, and what a platform team can do about it. I checked the pages below on 2026-10-21.

## What changed in October 2026

Key point

Two large providers raised GPU prices within a week of each other, reversing the 2025 trend.

The Uvik GPU Price Index (captured 7 October 2026) lists the dated events. On 1 October, Nebius raised H100 on-demand from $3.85 to $4.50 (+17%). It raised H200 from $4.50 to $5.40 (+20%). On 7 October, AWS raised EC2 Capacity Blocks prices by about 15%.

The Nebius pricing page I fetched today matches the new numbers. It lists H100 at $4.50, H200 at $5.40, B200 at $8.50 and B300 at $9.50 per GPU-hour. It also says prices may change at any time.

IntuitionLabs checked AWS on 10 October 2026. The Capacity Blocks rate for P5 (H100) is $5.970 per GPU. In July 2026 it was $5.191 in US regions and $4.720 in other regions. By my calculation from those figures, that is about +15% in the US and about +26.5% elsewhere. AWS says the rates are next scheduled to be updated in January 2027.

Note

Capacity Blocks are reservations, not on-demand. IntuitionLabs warns against using them for cross-provider comparison. AWS on-demand prices did not change in this round.

The earlier trend matters too. AWS cut on-demand prices by 44% for P5 (H100) in June 2025. Then the SemiAnalysis one-year H100 contract index rose from $1.70 to $2.35 per GPU-hour between October 2025 and March 2026. That is +38%. IntuitionLabs attributes a roughly 40% contract rise to HBM3e cost pass-throughs from Samsung and SK Hynix. That is the article's explanation, not a statement from the providers.

...

1 Prices fell with the June 2025 AWS cut of 44%, then rose: the one-year contract index went from $1.70 to $2.35, Nebius moved H100 from $3.85 to $4.50, and AWS Capacity Blocks rose about 15%.

...

The Uvik index covers 19 providers and 87 public on-demand prices. It excludes spot, marketplace, reserved and contract-only prices. For the H100 SXM it found a median of $4.20, a low of $3.20 (Hyperstack and Thunder Compute) and a high of $12.29 (Microsoft Azure).

Split by type, the four hyperscalers had a median of $10.53. The 12 GPU clouds had a median of $3.95. That is a 2.7x gap. Across all GPUs in the index the hyperscaler multiple runs from 1.7x to 2.7x.

...

Commitments change the picture. Uvik says three-year commitments cut H100 prices by 56% to 57% at AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure. That narrows the hyperscaler gap, but only if you can predict three years of demand.

...

- After falling in 2025, GPU rental prices rose in 2026: on 1 October 2026 Nebius raised H100 on-demand from $3.85 to $4.50 (+17%) and H200 from $4.50 to $5.40; AWS raised EC2 Capacity Blocks by about 15% (a reservation product, not on-demand, which did not change; next update scheduled January 2027).
- The Uvik index (19 providers, 87 public on-demand prices) put the median H100 SXM at $4.20 per GPU-hour on 7 October, with a hyperscaler median of $10.53 versus $3.95 for 12 GPU clouds (2.7x). Three-year commitments cut H100 prices by 56% to 57% at the big three.
- Which provider you rent from matters more than the month you rent in.

results.title: H100 GPU Rental Prices Ended October at $3.00+ | Lines.com | Lines.com
results.author: Dr. Sarah Okonkwo
highlights:
H100 GPU rental prices settled at exactly $3.00 per GPU-hour on October 31, 2026, according to the Ornn Compute Price Index, triggering resolution of the $3.00+ outcome in this Polymarket market. The benchmark, which tracks transacted rental prices across the neocloud market, confirmed the figure at the daily 12:00 AM ET settle. The historical base rate suggests commodity compute benchmarks rarely land precisely at a threshold boundary, making this a statistically notable resolution.

...

## H100 Rental Prices Confirmed Above $3.00 at October Close

The Ornn Compute Price Index (OCPI-H100) settled at $3.00 per GPU-hour on October 31, 2026, the final day of the resolution window. The index tracks exclusively transacted rental prices across neocloud providers, not list prices or estimates, making it a transaction-based benchmark. The $3.00 figure satisfied the market’s top outcome bracket, which required end-of-October pricing to reach or exceed that level. Earlier in October, the OCPI-H100 had settled at $2.79 per GPU-hour on October 2, meaning prices climbed roughly 7.5% across the month before hitting the threshold.

The broader provider landscape corroborated the index reading. Runpod listed H100 SXM at $3.99 per hour. Lambda’s 8-GPU H100 SXM instance listed at $3.99 per GPU-hour, up from $2.99 in a prior snapshot. Market-median pricing across all providers ranged from $3.25 to $3.28 per hour in September, establishing an upward trajectory into October. The data tells a clear story: neocloud supply remained tight enough relative to AI compute demand to sustain prices above the $3.00 benchmark through month-end.

The final probability at close reached 100.0%, converging from an opening-day price of 35 cents. A 10.7% single-day move on October 31 reflected the market absorbing the imminent settlement confirmation. The trajectory was not a gradual drift but a decisive repricing as the resolution window closed.

...

The $3.00+ outcome opened at 35 cents implied probability, meaning traders initially assessed roughly a one-in-three chance that H100 spot prices would reach the top bracket by October’s end. That opening price was a significant underestimate. The Ornn OCPI-H100 had already settled at $2.92 per GPU-hour on October 1, just $0.08 below the resolution threshold, and the broader market median sat at $3.25 to $3.28 per hour in September. Within the confidence interval of available data, the market underpriced the $3.00+ outcome at inception by a measurable margin.

...

How did H100 rental prices shift during October 2026?

The Ornn OCPI-H100 settled at $2.79 on October 2, rising to $3.00 by October 31, a gain of roughly 7.5% across the month. A 10.7% single-day move on October 31 reflected final market convergence as settlement approached.

results.title: The GPU Price Crash of 2025 and Why It Reversed - AIVory
results.author: Paul Piper
highlights:
By late 2025, one-year contract rates for H100s had fallen to $1.70/hr - a 75-80% crash from peak. Spot prices on marketplaces like Vast.ai dipped below $1.85/hr. Lambda Labs was listing on-demand H100s at $2.99-$3.99/hr while AWS still charged $6.88/hr for the same card.

The oversupply was real. Brokers who had pre-purchased thousands of GPUs were renting them at a loss just to cover power bills.

...

| Provider | Type | Mid-2025 ($/hr) | Mid-2026 ($/hr) | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AWS (p5.48xlarge) | On-demand | $6.88 | $6.98 | +1.5% |
| Lambda Labs | On-demand | $2.99 | $3.99 | +33% |
| CoreWeave | 1-year contract | $1.70 | ~$2.40 | +41% |
| Vast.ai | Spot | $1.85 | $2.50-3.20 | +35-73% |
| Nvidia DGX Cloud | On-demand | ~$3.70 | ~$4.40 | +19% |

...

## The reversal: 2026

Three things happened at once.

Nvidia raised the floor. In early 2026, Nvidia announced roughly a 20% price increase on H100 rental rates through its DGX Cloud and partner programs. That reset the baseline for everyone downstream.

Blackwell demand ate the surplus. New model architectures - reasoning models, multi-modal systems, long-context inference - need more compute per query. The University of Rhode Island measured GPT-5 class queries at 18.35 Wh average versus 2.12 Wh for GPT-4. That is 8.6x more energy per query, which translates directly to more GPU-hours consumed per dollar of API revenue.

Training runs got bigger again. Frontier labs resumed large pre-training runs on Blackwell clusters. That pulled supply out of the rental market. Blackwell spot rates jumped 48% in 60 days - from $2.75/hr to $4.08/hr.

One-year H100 contracts climbed roughly 40% off their late-2025 lows. The crash was over.

...

The 2023-2025 crash was a supply overshoot. The 2026 reversal is demand catching up. Neither was permanent.

Blackwell supply will ramp through late 2026 and into 2027. When it does, expect another pricing correction downward - probably not as steep as the H100 crash, because Nvidia learned from the oversupply cycle and is managing allocation more tightly.
